TumorLensCase SYN-07

A millimetre can change the call.

After glioblastoma surgery, a patient has an MRI every few months and someone measures what is left of the tumor. TumorLens measured 350 real follow-up calls from the LUMIERE dataset with two segmentation tools. A uniform 1 mm offset of every tumor edge changed 17% of one tool's calls and 28% of the other's.

Data LUMIERE, 91 patientsCriteria RANO, bidimensionalTools 2, compared
Scroll for a synthetic walk-through, then the real results
1 / 6Before surgery

A 38 mm enhancing mass in the right frontoparietal lobe.

Glioblastoma is the most common malignant brain tumor in adults. On a contrast-enhanced T1 scan it lights up where the blood–brain barrier is broken. Treatment starts with surgery to remove as much of it as is safe.

2 / 6After surgery

What remains is a cavity, a thin rim, and a nodule.

The rim around the cavity is not measured. RANO only counts solid enhancing tissue at least 10 × 10 mm. After six weeks of radiotherapy with temozolomide, the first scan becomes the baseline.

3 / 6Follow-up

A scan every eight weeks, measured the same way each time.

Find the axial slice where the nodule is largest. Measure its longest diameter, then the longest diameter perpendicular to it, and multiply. The smallest product so far is the nadir. Growth of 25% above the nadir means progression.

Nadir here: 195 mm² at week 16.

4 / 6Two models

Two segmentation models trace the edge. They disagree.

Where both models include the tissue, it is solid white. Where only one does, it glows amber. At week 32 their edges sit up to 0.80 mm apart.

5 / 6The decision

Stable on paper. Too close to call.

At week 32 the nodule measures 16.7 × 13.5 mm, 15.0% above the nadir. That is under the 25% line, so the call is stable disease.

Moving the edge outward by 0.27 mm would make it progression, and the models disagree by more than that. The call is decided by less than the gap between two reasonable outlines.

6 / 6On real scans

On LUMIERE, a uniform 1 mm edge offset changes 17 to 28% of calls.

Both released segmentations were measured on every visit and turned into RANO calls, then every edge in a patient's series was moved by the same amount. Bars show the share of 350 calls per tool that change.

Against the expert's own measurements, HD-GLIO-AUTO volume moved in the same direction in 84% of consecutive pairs, numerically similar to the 81% Suter et al. reported with a different tool, not a replication. Under this study's measuring conventions, automated sizes ran about 1.2 to 1.4 times the expert's. The 110 expert-measured visits are 106 progression and 4 partial response, so this describes progression scans, not response assessment in general.

Descriptive methods study of measurement-driven calls, not a validation of clinical response assessment; analysis rules were committed before results, and an independent review was run. Full numbers and limits: v1 results. Acts 1 to 5 use a synthetic patient.
